messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Henry had always been a man who took pride in his ability to stay calm under pressure. As a tutor, he was accustomed to helping students navigate challenging material and managing his own stress levels with ease. But all of that changed when the Category 5 hurricane tore through his coastal town two years ago. The storm had been predicted to make landfall hours later than it did, leaving Henry and his wife scrambling to secure their home and flee to safety. The howling winds and lashing rain created a maelstrom that seemed to go on forever, and when the waters finally receded, Henry's neighborhood was left in ruins. At first, Henry tried to tackle the cleanup efforts head-on, but as he worked through the wreckage of his home, memories of that terrifying night began to flood back. He would recall the sound of the wind screaming like a banshee outside, and then suddenly feel completely numb, as if it had all happened to someone else. Other times, the smell of saltwater and mud would transport him back to that desperate, clinging-to-life moment when the storm surge threatened to engulf their home. As the memories resurfaced, Henry found himself ruminating on how they could have prevented the damage – if only they'd boarded up the windows sooner, or evacuated earlier. He'd spend hours going over every decision, wondering what he could've done differently. It was as if by replaying that fateful night in his mind, he could somehow prevent it from happening again. But this constant dwelling on what might have been took a toll. Henry started to feel like the universe was conspiring against him – when something took longer than expected, he'd assume the worst, convinced that disaster lurked just around the corner. He'd scan every room he entered for potential dangers, positioning himself with his back against a wall so he could keep an eye out for any signs of trouble. As time went on, Henry's fixation on safety began to affect his daily life as a tutor. He started avoiding teaching sessions that might take place in unfamiliar locations or at odd hours – the uncertainty was just too much to handle. His wife grew concerned about the changes she saw in him, but Henry reassured her that he just needed some more time to process what had happened. Yet even with all his efforts to avoid stressors, the memories continued to force their way into his mind, often at the most inopportune moments – during sessions with students, or while trying to relax at home. When this happened, Henry would dissociate from the recollections, pretending they'd happened to someone else – it was the only way he knew how to cope. The loop of memories, ruminations, and fears began to tighten its grip on Henry's life. He became increasingly withdrawn, struggling to connect with his students or enjoy time with his wife. It wasn't until a particularly difficult session with a student – one where Henry had dissociated so completely that he barely remembered what they'd discussed – that he realized something was very wrong. Henry confided in his wife about how overwhelmed he felt, and together they decided it was time to seek help. As he sat in the therapist's office for their first appointment, Henry couldn't shake the feeling of being trapped, with the weight of those memories pressing down on him like a physical force. He knew that breaking free from this cycle would be no easy task – but for the sake of his relationships and his own sanity, he was willing to try.
